interest: This file offers valuable historical insight into the economic policies and industrial reorientation of Japan during the Allied Occupation (1946–1949). The detailed report by H. Wickliffe Rose reveals the dramatic impact of wartime rationalization and machinery scrapping—which eliminated far more rayon productive capacity than Allied bombing raids—and documents ground-level technological adaptations, such as chemical substitutions for scarce caustic soda and integrated pulp-to-garment manufacturing. Furthermore, the 1949 correspondence regarding India's unsuccessful requests for silkworm eggs highlights the geopolitics of postwar trade and Asian textile competition: it explicitly exposes SCAP's protective strategy of safeguarding traditional Japanese industries like sericulture from foreign competition to ensure Japan's economic revival, even at the expense of newly independent Asian nations like India.
overview: Decimal file 894.6132 (May 1946 – July 1949) documents U.S. State Department and SCAP monitoring, regulation, and rehabilitation of Japan's agricultural and industrial fiber industries during the early Allied Occupation. The file centers on raw fiber supply, synthetic textile capacity, and international trade controls, encompassing: an extensive May 1946 address and survey report by H. Wickliffe Rose of the State-Army Textile Mission evaluating the wartime destruction, scrapping, and post-war revival of Japan's rayon industry; late 1946 correspondence concerning American commercial inquiries on ramie imports under Allied trade restrictions via the U.S. Commercial Company; a March 1948 State Department economic assessment of Japan's abaca (Manila hemp) import requirements for fisheries and transportation; and a July 1949 diplomatic despatch with SCAP memoranda detailing the rejection of Indian diplomatic requests to purchase Japanese silkworm eggs and seeds to develop India's and Jammu and Kashmir's sericulture industries, illustrating SCAP's protective stance toward traditional Japanese export industries.

subfiles.about: Covering letter transmitting a copy of H. Wickliffe Rose's address on the Japanese rayon industry following his participation in the Textile Mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rebecca H. Morton, assistant to H. Wickliffe Rose at American Viscose Corporation, writes to Clair Wilcox, Director of the State Department's Office of International Trade Policy. She forwards a copy of Rose's recent address to the American Association of Textile Technologists regarding the rayon industry in Japan. A handwritten marginal notation indicates internal State Department circulation and coordination.
subfiles.title: Letter from Rebecca H. Morton to Clair Wilcox transmitting address on Japanese rayon industry

subfiles.about: Comprehensive speech delivering technical, economic, and operational observations on the Japanese rayon industry following the State-Army Textile Mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: H. Wickliffe Rose recounts his survey of Japan's rayon industry as part of the Allied Textile Mission in early 1946. He outlines the mission's itinerary, interactions with SCAP and Japanese industry officials, and findings on productive capacity, revealing that wartime scrapping reduced capacity from 1.6 billion pounds registered in 1939 to an actual potential capacity of 354 million pounds. He examines technical practices, including chemical processes, quality testing at the Yokohama experimental station, university research at Kyoto, and factory visits, noting that coal and raw material shortages constrain current production. Rose concludes that while Japan will not rapidly flood global markets, moderate rehabilitation under Allied occupation is progressing cooperatively.
subfiles.title: Address by H. Wickliffe Rose on 'The Rayon Industry of Japan'

subfiles.about: Inquiry from an American businessman regarding the availability and quotation of ramie fiber and grass imports from Japan.
subfiles.summary: P. J. Leavitt of Hartford, Connecticut writes to Edwin M. Martin at the State Department's Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs. Leavitt seeks commercial information on importing ramie (Chinese linen) from Japan in both finished spinning fiber and raw grass/ribbon forms. He asks for guidance and suggestions on where and how to obtain quotations and procure the fiber.
subfiles.title: Letter from P. J. Leavitt to Edwin M. Martin requesting information on ramie imports from Japan

subfiles.about: Reply explaining Occupation trade regulations and directing private ramie import inquiries to the U.S. Commercial Company.
subfiles.summary: Edwin M. Martin replies to P. J. Leavitt explaining that direct private commercial trade with Japan is currently prohibited under Occupation policy. He states that all Japanese import procurement is managed through the U.S. Commercial Company, an RFC subsidiary, and provides their Washington address. Martin notes that difficulties in reviving the Japanese ramie industry have prevented recent exports, but encourages Leavitt to submit detailed requirements to the agency for future scheduling.
subfiles.title: Letter from Edwin M. Martin to P. J. Leavitt concerning ramie imports and U.S. Commercial Company

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum evaluating Japanese import requirements and factory capacity for abaca (Manila hemp).
subfiles.summary: Miss Baldwin assesses Japan's abaca import requirement of 78,500,000 pounds for fiscal year 1949, comparing it to pre-war consumption averages (1935–1938) and current industrial capacities. The memo breaks down domestic needs among fisheries, civil communications, and transportation, noting that rope processing capacity currently stands at 60,000,000 pounds annually. Baldwin also evaluates pre-war export statistics from the Philippines and comments from the Oriental Economist regarding Japanese fishing industry demands.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum from Miss Baldwin to Mr. Evans on Japanese abaca requirements

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting correspondence regarding SCAP's rejection of Indian requests to import silkworm eggs from Japan.
subfiles.from: Office of the U.S. Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The Acting U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo transmits three memoranda concerning an Indian government request to acquire Japanese silkworm eggs for sericulture development. The despatch summarizes SCAP's conclusion that no silkworm eggs are available for export. Crucially, the Political Adviser observes that GHQ SCAP continues to view with mistrust any attempt by foreign competitors to establish rival operations against traditional Japanese industries like sericulture.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 481 from U.S. Political Adviser, Tokyo, on export of silkworm eggs to India

subfiles.about: Indian Liaison Mission request to SCAP for parent silkworm eggs (P2 eggs) of four original Japanese races for experimental breeding.
subfiles.summary: J. Chatterjee, Trade Registrar of the Indian Liaison Mission in Tokyo, submits an official request to SCAP's Economic and Scientific Section to procure 25–30 moths of four original silkworm races (P2 eggs). He notes the historical popularity of Japanese strains in India and cites the Japanese Raw Silk Industry Law governing export prohibitions. The Mission asks SCAP to examine the request to aid the development and improvement of Indian sericulture.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Indian Liaison Mission requesting silkworm eggs for experimental purposes
subfiles.to: Chief, Scientific and Technical Division, ESS, GHQ, SCAP

subfiles.about: Follow-up memorandum requesting 1,000 ounces of univoltine silkworm seeds for the Government of Jammu and Kashmir.
subfiles.summary: Following up on his unanswered April memorandum, J. Chatterjee conveys an additional urgent request from the Government of India for 1,000 ounces of Jan White univoltine silkworm seeds. The seeds are requested specifically on behalf of the Government of Jammu and Kashmir to support regional sericulture development. He asks SCAP's Foreign Trade and Commerce Division to facilitate the release and export of the requested silkworm strains.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Indian Liaison Mission requesting silkworm seeds for Jammu and Kashmir
subfiles.to: Chief, Scientific and Technical Division, ESS, GHQ, SCAP

subfiles.about: SCAP notification detailing prior discussions with Mr. Venkatarao and officially denying silkworm egg export to India due to domestic shortages.
subfiles.summary: R. D. Cleaves, Chief of SCAP's Textile Division, responds to the Indian Liaison Mission's requests of April 11 and July 1, 1949. He recounts that Indian representative H. S. Venkatarao had previously discussed the matter in June and was verbally informed after consultation with the Japanese Government that eggs were unavailable due to acute domestic shortages. Cleaves confirms that no written reply was sent earlier at Venkatarao's request, but officially reiterates that no silkworm eggs or seeds can be spared for export.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from SCAP Textile Division rejecting Indian request for silkworm eggs
subfiles.to: Head of the Indian Liaison Mission in Japan
